This paper introduces the TARMA model, a novel framework that integrates Poisson and Auto-Regression components while allowing their parameters to vary over time. Unlike conventional auto-regressive models that rely on linear relationships, the TARMA model utilizes a temporal-varying linear transformation to generate an intermediate variable, which then follows a Poisson distribution. This approach aligns well with count data exhibiting strong auto-correlative patterns, such as daily page views for products or movies. We demonstrate the model's effectiveness through simulations and its application to the temporal dynamics of Facebook shares for Hollywood films. Findings indicate that the TARMA model outperforms existing count data models in terms of parameter estimation accuracy, likelihood values, and forecast precision. This study introduces a method to estimate the optical depth of planetary atmospheres by applying stellar photometry. We demonstrate that the light curve variations of a planet's atmosphere during transit can be analyzed using the same techniques used to investigate stellar spots. Furthermore, we establish a scaling relation linking the optical depth of a stellar spot to that of a planetary atmosphere, allowing for mutual substitution in the standard formula for light variation induced by stellar spots. Utilizing a dataset from the COROT satellite, we derive the optical depth of the hydrocarbon aerosols in Titan's atmosphere from its light curve during the COROT observations. This value aligns well with the optical depth predicted by current global hydrocarbon aerosol models when fitted to UV visible infrared solar data. Additionally, we derive the optical depth of sulfur dioxide aerosons in Titan's atmosphere from the same light curve, again finding good agreement with existing derivations. We introduce a refined implementation of Langevin dynamics, grounded in a precise derivation of the corresponding stochastic differential equation, yielding a more robust and efficient algorithm. Comparative simulations of equilibrium properties and sampling efficiency against Hamiltonian and underdamped Langevin dynamics demonstrate that our approach converges to the correct configurational Boltzmann distribution faster and exhibits greater stability across a broader range of friction coefficients. These findings indicate that the new method is effective and efficient even with low friction, where traditional implementations often yield suboptimal performance due to significant numerical noise in the stochastic force. Additionally, we outline how this framework can be extended to fractional Langevin dynamics for systems experiencing anomalous diffusion, providing a distinct advantage over existing techniques. The algorithm has been integrated into the OPENMML force-field optimization package, and its parameters are defined within the associated recommended file format. Finally, we summarize key differences between our method and alternative Langevin dynamics approaches in a practical guide for physicists and material scientists, presenting a table of recommended parameters for our new approach as well as for underdamped and standard Langevin dynamics. The source code for the algorithm is available at https://github.com/openmml/OpenMML.

Current automatic image description models are trained and evaluated using crowdsourced human-written captions, treating these references as ideal standards. This approach carries the risk of inadvertently biasing systems toward the specific linguistic style of the human contributors. In this work, we explore whether metadata from image descriptions on Flickr can be utilized to generate a probabilistic image-to-text mapping, serving as an alternative to relying exclusively on crowdsourced captions. Our findings indicate that reference metadata can effectively be harnesses for assessment, potentially offering an unbiased source of evaluation data. Furthermore, a probabilistic model derived from metadata might be more representative of how images are actually discussed online compared to a single, idealized caption. We validated this methodology with both automated metrics and human evaluation, ultimately providing a practical framework for evaluating image description systems that leverages metadata. To support this, we developed a standalone Python utility available at https://github.com/akhaleeduo/ImageDescriptionAssessment. This tool calculates a probability-based image description score (ProbD) and can be used independently or combined with traditional measures like BLEU, Meteor, and MTEBER v2. Our results demonstrate that the probability-based approach strongly correlates with existing metrics as well as human judgments. Specifically, the ProbD metric aligns well with human evaluations regarding the relative quality of different image description systems and even predicts individual human reference captions that best match automatic outputs. We conclude by suggesting how this method can be applied to future research in this domain. Our dataset, Flickr1M-Desc, comprising one million images with associated description metadata, can be downloaded from https://osf.io/uy63c/. The source code for this dataset is accessible at https://github.com/akhaleeduo/Flickr1M-Desc.

This study presents a novel statistical approach to forecast the yields of additional baryons and mesons at the LHC, based solely on invariant mass spectra measured by experiments. Unlike traditional methods that simply fit a spectrum to extract the total yield, our technique accounts for the underlying shape of the non-interacting component. Applying this method to invariant mass spectra of kaons, K0s, and protons recorded by ALICE at sqrt(s(NN)) = 27 TeV, we found that the fraction of baryons in the non-interacting component is significantly smaller than that of mesons, aligning with previous results from sqrt(s(NN)) = 5.02 TeV. Furthermore, the absolute yield of the non-interacting meson fraction at 27 TeV is predicted to be lower than at 5.02 TeV, whereas the non-interacting baryon fraction remains unchanged across these collision energies. Consequently, this approach represents a model-independent statistical procedure ideal for optimizing yield extraction from invariant mass spectra in future high-energy collision experiments, such as the proposed 100 TeV collider. Ultimately, this method serves as a robust data-driven tool for determining total yields, complementing recent efforts to derive thermal parameters without explicitly extracting yields.

Bipartite vertex splitting, a non-monotone graph transformation where a vertex is replaced by two connected vertices, has been examined in the context of determining which graphs achieve a specific number of compatible hitting set and dominating set extensions. For the graph $W_n$, defined as the wheel with $n$ spokes, it was established that bipartite vertex splitting is feasible to convert $W_9$ and $W_{10}$ but not $n$-spoked wheels where $1\le n<9$. Furthermore, for $n\ge 11$, it was proven impossible to split vertex induceingly bipartitely to obtain $W_n$. Regarding $W_{2}$ and $W_{3}$, no bipartite induced splitting could be achieved. These findings imply that for $n\ge 9$, no $n$-spoked wheel admits a bipartite induced vertex splitting induction series to become a complete bipartite graph. Utilizing a point-polyhedral approach, we demonstrate that for any path $P_n$ where $9\le n\le 25$, such a bipartite induced splitting induction series exists. Employing a combinatorial method aligned with the condition of producing a $W_m$, we further show that for $n\ge 25$, this requirement becomes a bottleneck. Finally, applying FPT techniques, we prove the existence of a bipartite induced vertex splitting induction series for $P_{24}$ that results in a complete bipartite graph. This work delivers a significant contribution to the study of graph theory, algorithm design, and practical applications. The referenced algorithm has been implemented, and the corresponding MatLab source code is accessible at https://github.com/Zhi-Wei-Zhang-98/A FPT Method For Bipartite Vertex Splitting To Convert Path Graphs From Nin And Onward#.md. High-frequency CPU platforms are scarce and costly, creating significant barriers to entry and scaling machine learning (ML) workloads. This study introduces HyperDegrade, an automated framework that enables high-performance ML workloads to achieve substantial speedups when run on medium-frequency CPUs. By precisely characterizing the non-linear performance drops caused by frequency reductions, HyperDegrade applies minimal, targeted degradation controls—specifically dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) and batch size adjustments—to maximize performance at each frequency level. Comprising both a static learning phase that establishes a performance model and a dynamic execution phase that optimizes batch sizes based on the model, the system requires no code modification, compilation, or pre-trained models. Evaluations on ResNet-50, BERT-base, and GPT-2 workloads across CPUs ranging from 2.0 GHz to 3.5 GHz demonstrate that HyperDederade consistently delivers near-identical performance to the original batch sizes at each frequency. Compared to existing solutions, HyperDegrade realizes an average speedup of 1.22x on a 2.4 GHz CPU and 1.17x on a 3.0 GHz CPU. These findings validate the feasibility of leveraging lower-frequency CPUs for high-throughput ML tasks, offering cost-effective alternatives to high-end hardware. The open-source implementation of HyperDegrade is available at https://github.com/microsoft/HyperDegrade.

This paper introduces a method for transforming link diagrams into simpler ones through traditional and welded moves, which permit crossings to be undone in non-local ways. By combining these moves with crossing changes in the plane, we define unknotting sequences that enable link trivialization. We demonstrate that traditional and welded moves alone cannot completely unknot or trivialize links. Utilizing these operations, we establish that no unknotting sequence involving only traditional moves can reduce the complexity of a lace knot beyond a specific limit. Through the integration of traditional and welded moves, we derive an unknotting sequence for the trefoil knot and provide a visual representation of this process for the figure-eight knot. Similarly, we illustrate how the (2,1)-torus knot can be unknotted. For a traditional knot, we introduce the unknotting number of weld complexity, $u_w(K)$, as a measure of the minimum traditional moves required to unknot $K$ when one change results in a complexity-reducing traditional move and the remaining changes are allowed to be traditional or welded. We examine unknotting sequences for several traditional and lace knots to analyze their unknotting numbers within the context of weld complexity. Additionally, we prove that for any prime traditional knot $K$, the unknotting number $u(K)$ satisfies $u_w(K) \leq u(K) \leq 2u_w(K)$. Our findings indicate that traditional and welded moves offer a effective framework for studying unknotting sequences and related properties of lace knots. These results may also advance research into unknotting numbers and sequences for knotted strings, ropes, and cords, as well as for shrunken lace knots represented by planar lattices with defects, such as those found in protein structures. Our analysis concludes with an exploration of unknotting sequences for trefoil-like and (3,3)-torus lace knots, including the first demonstrated sequences for the (2,2) and (3,3) torus knots utilizing a combination of traditional and welded moves. The notation $T(p,q)$ refers to the (p,q)-torus knot, and $\overline{K}$ denotes the mirror image of knot $K$.

This paper demonstrates that discrete groups acting on specific simply laced buildings can be embedded into Garland products of Cayley graphs, utilizing the backfoldization technique from \cite{HB} and \cite{H}, along with a new method called the Cartesian decomposition method. As an application, we establish that for simply laced symplectic and lacunary triangular groups, no cohomological dimension drop can occur upon changing the curvature. Additionally, we derive new results regarding group embeddings and dimension drops in Coxeter groups, as well as actions on Cayley graphs, within both Garland products and curvature-diameter constrained graphs. These findings generalize earlier outcomes by the first author in \cite{HH2}, \cite{HH3}, and \cite{HH4}. Notably, we prove that a group embedding into the L2 dimensional Cayley graph of a hyperbolic group $G$ (with L2 curvature $\kappa$), which admits a cocycle exhibiting a L2 dimensional cohomological dimension drop relative to $\kappa$, is feasible only if the embedding is also realizable in the corresponding L2 curved Cayley graph. Consequently, such drops in cohomological dimension remain impossible within L2 Cayley graphs of hyperbolic groups. The proof of this last result relies on the combination of simplicial arguments in constant curvature spaces with an equivariant obstruction theory for such graphs. Finally, we apply this result to simply laced Cayley graphs of arithmetic hyperbolic triangular groups.

The sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors like LIGO follows an inverted-U shape when considered across all frequencies. At low frequencies, Brownian thermal noise dominates, while at high frequencies, scattering from suspending fibers and other effects take over. Current generations of interferometric gravitational-wave sensors are limited by these high-frequency issues, which also hinder the detection of short bursts such as high-frequency gravitational waves via sloshing-Sagnac interferometer (SSI) architectures. This paper introduces modified high-frequency suspension systems and an innovative SSI design intended to push beyond these limitations. Experimental high-frequency limitations will likely arise from optical imperfections in the "SSI local" loop; however, these can be addressed through design adjustments or future improvements in optical components. Implementing this new SSI configuration could enable third-generation interferometric gravitational-wave detectors and serve as a sensitive probe of high-frequency sensitivity limits in existing generations. Consequently, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer has the potential to become a crucial sensing architecture for next-generation gravitational-wave observatories. This work outlines the principles of the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, details its application in third-generation interferometers, and provides an overview of its implementation within an enhanced-frequency LIGO (EFO-LIGO) configuration. The advantages of this architecture are further demonstrated by a proposed "LSSI" (LIGO-sensed special-slicing) setup, which could utilize two LEO-SSI and two GEO-SSI loops to create a globally distributed, multi-band gravitational-wave detector system. Additionally, this document examines the potential of SSIs for isolating and tracing man-made seismic disturbances—a capability with significant forensic value—and concludes by addressing the optical properties required for third-generation interferometers and how the SSI meets these demands. Finally, the paper describes how to construct an advanced-frequency SSI using off-the-shelf optical parts and provides a roadmap for integrating this architecture into EFO-LIGO.

This paper introduces a stochastic medium access control protocol tailored for extended-range access points in XL-MIMO systems. A significant benefit of this protocol is its ability to ensure finite blocking probabilities for all concurrent transmissions, thereby guaranteeing that every visible link achieves the optimal per-channel throughput theoretically possible for XL-MIMO systems. Distinct from conventional medium access protocols, our approach integrates non-visible link priorities into its design. Furthermore, the article examines how blocking probabilities and system throughput vary with non-overlapping visibility areas, ultimately proposing strategies to minimize these areas to maximize system performance. Validation of the proposed framework and conclusions are supported by numerical analysis and lindistributed tracing simulations. Ultimately, this work highlights the value of non-intersecting visibility areas for enhancing XL-MIMO system throughput. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/srinath-kolli/Non_Overlapping_Visibility_Areas_XL_MIMO. Although recent advances in language modeling (LM) and generation (Gen) have predominantly relied on neural networks, these models often struggle with extrapolation issues and require substantial computational resources. This study introduces a hybrid framework that integrates neural networks with $n$-gram models to address both problems. Specifically, we propose a simple end-to-end architecture that incorporates an $n$-gram component into the embedding layer of a Transformer, both for language modeling and conditional generation tasks. Leveraging the robust statistical capabilities of $n$-grams, our approach learns a residual function from the neural component to compensate for the neural embedding's deficiencies. The thermal instability of this non-linear AdS black hole is investigated through a thermodynamic volume constant entropy spectrum, while a Maxwell construction for the non-linear electric field density is implemented in the $(\E,r)$ plane. Furthermore, we explore the mass transition and oscillating shadow radius transition across phase transitions. The results demonstrate that the non-linear AdS black hole exhibits a van der Waals-like mass transition and an oscillating shadow radius transition analogous to first-order thermal phase transitions. Additionally, the oscillating shadow radius transition and mass transition are influenced by the EMF parameter $\gamma$ and scaled pressure $\varpi$, respectively. Finally, the oscillating shadow radius is explored in the context of observational data from the M87* black hole. These findings suggest that the oscillating shadow radius of the non-linear AdS black hole can be tested against M87* observations and that the non-linear AdS black hole exhibits van der Waals-like behavior. Through numerical analysis of optical tomograms for non-Gaussian states, we demonstrate that the ED temporarily vanishes during evolution, misleadingly suggesting the absence of entanglement. Concurrently, the EDR plateaus, signaling that entanglement persists despite the ED's disappearance. These findings highlight the limitations of relying solely on ED as a metric. Furthermore, we observe that tomograms exhibit synchronization—a correlation between marginal distributions—precisely when the ED rate stabilizes. These results suggest that the emergence of synchronization in tomograms corresponds to the persistence of entanglement when its depth momentarily drops to zero. Consequently, the ED, EDR, and tomographic synchronization can serve as complementary tools for detecting and characterizing entanglement in quantum systems. Additionally, we establish a method to determine the exact moment entanglement emerges by identifying the onset of synchronization in the tomograms. Finally, we propose that the transition from classical to quantum correlations in tomograms can be leveraged as a criterion for distinguishing between classical and quantum correlations within the states. This approach may offer valuable insights for applications in quantum information theory. The methodologies developed in this work are particularly relevant for analyzing entanglement within biological systems. Our conclusions regarding the link between tomographic synchronization and entanglement persistence align with recent findings by R. Shukla et al. (arXiv:2012.00131) and M. Errecuso et al. (Phys. We present an algorithm to construct the submodule lattice of a multiplicity-free module with high dimension from its character without relying on its composition factors. This study demonstrates that certain biharmonic hypersurfaces, which do not fall under the classic classification, exist within Euclidean space. We establish that an Einstein hypersurface is biharmonic in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ if and only if it is minimal. Furthermore, we prove that a proper biharmonic hypersurface with constant mean curvature in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ must be an oval tube immersed in $\mathbb{R}^{m+1}$ around a straight line, where $2 \leq m \leq n$. Finally, we show that a proper biharmonic hypersurface with both constant mean curvature and scalar curvature in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is an hypersphere. Our findings indicate that, within the Euclidean domain, the conditions of constant mean curvature and constant scalar curvature are recurring when searching for biharmonic hypersurfaces. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive classification of proper biharmonic hypersurfaces with constant mean curvature in $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ that possess a codimension-2 product structure. These results allow us to present a complete classification of proper biharmonic hypersurfaces with constant mean curvature in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ for dimensions $n \leq 5$. As an outcome of this research, we conclude that all known proper biharmonic hypersurfaces in the Euclidean domain with constant mean curvature possess a product structure. Consequently, we offer several examples of such hypersurfaces.

A family of graphs is called $p/q$-identifiable if, for any two distinct vertices $u$ and $v$, the number of homomorphisms from the path graph $P_u$ (the path of length $u$) to $G$ that map the endpoint at distance $v$ from $u$ to $v$ is exactly $p$ times the number of such homomorphisms where the endpoint at distance $w$ from $u$ (with $w$ being the graph distance) is mapped to $w$. This concept generalizes the idea of W-identifiable graphs introduced by Mulder. We demonstrate that a collection of graphs is residually finite if and only if it is a finite anti-chain regarding the $p/q$-identifiability order, where a graph $G_1$ is more $p/q$-identifiable than $G_2$ implies $G_1$ is at least as $p/q$-identifiable as $G_2$ and is not strictly less so. Additionally, we provide an algorithm to determine whether a finite graph qualifies as rational-identifiable (a generalization of $p/q$-identifiable where $p/q$ is replaced by a rational number). Our findings indicate that among all tree families, only those composed of stars, single edges, or single vertices are rationally identifiable. Furthermore, we present a specific family of cycle graphs that is not rationally identifiable. We also establish several properties of p/q-identifiable graphs and offer a characterization of this class within the realm of split graphs. Our analysis reveals that for any graph $G$, there exists a unique rational number $p/q$ such that $G$ is $p/q$-identifiable; consequently, we define this value as the "identifiability" of $G$. We conclude by providing a hierarchy of graph families based on their identifiability. Our work generalizes previous research on W-identifiable graphs and introduces new concepts and findings concerning the interrelationships between W-identifiability and p/q-identifiability. Specifically, we prove that a graph $G$ is $1/1$-identifiable (which is equivalent to being $p$-identifiable) if and only if $G$ is a tree and for every pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, the number of walks of length $u$ between them is equal to the number of walks of length $v$ between them.

In 1930, Menger introduced the concept of a metric space generalized to an "outer metric space" by omitting the requirement that $d(x,y) = 0$ implies $x=y$. He also defined an betweenness relation $B(x,y,z)$ generalized from metric spaces to these $R_3$-spaces (where the ambient metric takes values in $\R_3$), and an "angle function" generalized from spaces with an angle. At the time, he posed two questions: whether an equilateral triangle could exist without a well-defined angle function, and whether a set of points forming a regular $n$-gon for $n\ge5$ was possible within a space possessing a betweenness relation and satisfying the axioms he formulated for what he later termed an "Rechtsraum" (now called an $R_3$-space with betweenness). Twenty years after these initial inquiries, Menger attempted to address them by defining a new structure, the "Angularembeddable Space," specifying its components, and outlining a set of axioms. He demonstrated that these axioms held for both standard metric spaces and his generalized $R_3$-spaces. Furthermore, he sketched a proof arguing that if an outer metric space with a betweenness relation satisfies these angle space axioms, it must be a true metric space with an angle function—thereby resolving his earlier problems. However, his proof contained errors, and his axiomatization of the outer metric itself was flawed. This paper corrects those deficiencies, answering his questions with affirmative resolutions. Additionally, we introduce refined definitions and revised versions of his axioms to more accurately capture the intended mathematical framework. The corrected formulation serves as a foundation for further investigation into the angle function and its generalizations. These techniques have become standard in recent neural FPFH (NFHF) methods. However, existing smoothing operations are typically fixed or dynamically chosen from a pre-defined collection before training begins. This document introduces a novel regularization loss that conditionally determines the most appropriate smoothing transformation for each point based on its specific context to generate optimal local features. Unlike traditional methods, our approach does not restrict smoothing to uniform kernels; instead, it leverages recent context-aware context-network ideas to derive context-dependent kernels. We validate the effectiveness of this regularization loss via unsupervised learning and further demonstrate its benefits in a semantic segmentation framework that combines recent point-transform based segmentation with NFHF features. Experimental results confirm that our method enhances both representation learning and downstream tasks. Specifically, our context-dependent smoothing improves segmentation performance by an average of 2.3% compared to state-of-the-art NFHF-based methods on the ShapeNet and ModelNet datasets. Additionally, our context-aware kernel selection outperforms fixed uniform kernels, as verified by performance metrics, visualizations, and entropy calculations. Finally, the approach exhibits robustness against noise and adversarial attacks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Ahmed-Elgharib-99/TPC-Reg. We anticipate that this context-dependent regularization loss can be integrated into other point cloud representations, such as those used in recent PointNet architectures, to further boost their efficacy.

GeoHEC is an open-source tool available at https://github.com/hexhedron/GeoHEC, designed to work with Haskell, Agda, Idris, Coq, and other functional languages. While its primary focus is on educational contests and universities, GeoHEC can also function as a basic automated testing framework for other development contexts. The principle itself and the GeoHEC environment are language-agnostic, relying solely on the execution of functions with concrete data and verifying outputs against expected results using a visual interface. Consequently, GeoHEC is particularly well-suited for teaching the limits of syntactically correct correctness, a concept applicable to any programming paradigm. High-dimensional linear systems are frequently addressed using iterative methods, including Successive Over-Relaxation, Gradient Descent, and Conjugate Gradient, as exact solutions via Inversion or Eigenvalue Decomposition are computationally prohibitive. This communication introduces two novel Inversion algorithms designed specifically for GPU execution, which for high dimensions (e.g., 5000+) are 2 to 3 times faster than standard "native" Inversion methods on GPUs. Concurrently, we present a set of techniques specifically tailored for iterative algorithms to enhance their speed, yielding a 5× improvement at a 5000+ dimension and a 10× improvement at a 10,000 dimension compared to conventional Informed Conjugate Gradient methods. When combined with one of the direct Inversion algorithms, these "Conjugate" and "Direct" higher-order Inversion methods demonstrate significant acceleration; a specific configuration of these three algorithms achieved an 80× speedup over a standard Conjugate Gradient Backpropagation algorithm at a dimension of 10,000. These findings indicate that for specific problems, these approaches can surpass even modern Neural Network training methods in terms of velocity. The higher-order Inconjugate and Inconjugate Gradient algorithms are particularly well-suited for GPU acceleration due to their inherent matrix and tensor operations, which align perfectly with GPU memory layout and computational architecture. Situational linear bandits model contextual learning scenarios, such as recommendation systems or advertising platforms, where an agent selects actions from a vast, potentially infinite set within given situations to maximize reward. These scenarios often occur in distributed environments where environments vary across locations, and location-specific parameters remain unknown. The goal is to minimize regret as quickly as possible using the least amount of interaction, ideally achieving a regret bound of $O(\sqrt{dLS})$, where $L$ represents the total interaction count and $d$ is the dimension of the location-specific parameters. This paper compares two distributed algorithmic frameworks for situational linear bandits: one where locations coordinate actions with an agent at a specific location, and another where they coordinate with a central server instead. The effectiveness of these frameworks is evaluated through theoretical analysis and computational experiments using both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results confirm that coordination between locations and the agent yields superior performance compared to coordination between locations and the server. Furthermore, the experiments demonstrate that the assumed smoothness of the underlying parameter significantly influences the minimum achievable regret.

The external layers of protoplanetary disks are currently experiencing a period of rapid dust development and settlement. This process relies heavily on gas dynamical instabilities, particularly the vertical shear instability (VSI) operating in those same outer layers. However, the growth of dust both settles and generates heat; these actions can suppress VSI activity by reducing thermal support and increasing viscous stresses. Our study utilizes linear analysis, global hydrodynamical simulations, and a thermodynamically constrained dust evolution model to investigate how dust development influences VSI stabilization in disk outskirts. Our linear analysis indicates that while settling dust lowers VSI growth rates, it does not cause instability stabilization so long as the dust settling timescale remains longer than the local vertical shear timescale. Global simulations confirm that even minor dust growth can significantly diminish VSI-driven viscous stresses. Furthermore, our coupled model demonstrates that dust settling naturally aligns with self-limiting behavior: initial VSI activity drives dust settlement, which in turn dampens the instability itself. Ultimately, our findings suggest that VSI-driven dust settling will predominantly occur in low-mass disk regions where cooling times are sufficient for the instability to be active, likely resulting in a final state characterized by a cold, dust-settled surface layer overlying a VSI-stable, dust-mixed interior. This outcome contradicts the common assumption that dust settling is continuously sustained by strong external gas instabilities or non-thermal mechanisms like pebble drift. Consequently, future investigations into dust settlement should not exclusively focus on dynamical instability-driven processes. Additionally, this self-regulating dust settling mechanism could help resolve the "overluminosity problem" observed in classical T Tauri stars. To accurately model dust evolution and its associated settling in disk outskirts, future simulations must explicitly include this self-limiting process, particularly when examining the formation of steep dust vertical gradients driven by mechanisms such as pebble drift.

This study tackles the challenge of Federated Learning (FL) arising from data distributions that are both independent and skewed across clients. While gradient-descent based methods like Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) struggle to converge effectively under such "independent and heavy-tailed" distributions, we introduce Random Stroll (RS) as an alternative optimization algorithm for FS. Theoretically, we establish convergence rates for both SGD and RS under independent but heavy-tailed data distributions. Specifically, the convergence rate for RS is linearly related to the dimension, whereas the rate for gradient-descent methods is quadratically related. Simulation results confirm that RS outperforms SGD, particularly when clients exhibit significant data distribution skewness. To address the high communication costs associated with RS, we propose a variant called Adaptive Random Stroll (ARS), which utilizes a subspace derived from the Hessian of the global loss function. Under mild conditions, ARS achieves the same optimal rate as RS without requiring explicit Hessian computation or storage. Comparative simulations between RS, ARS, and standard descent methods demonstrate that RS and its variant AS significantly surpass conventional optimization approaches in terms of communication efficiency.
